school-c9-english-a.title: Class 9 English · Beehive Prose (Ch 1–5)
school-c9-english-a.description: Chapter-by-chapter study of Class 9 Beehive prose: The Fun They Had, The Sound of Music, The Little Girl, A Truly Beautiful Mind and The Snake and the Mirror — summaries in original words, themes, vocabulary, solved answers and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The Fun They Had
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Isaac Asimov's science-fiction story set in 2157: Margie and Tommy discover a printed book about old schools and wonder whether children of the past had more fun.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story in sequence
Learners can compare the mechanical teacher with human teachers
Learners can discuss the theme of technology and learning
Learners can answer short, long and extract-based questions in board format

scenes.text: In the year 2157, thirteen-year-old Tommy finds something strange in his attic: a real paper book.
Eleven-year-old Margie is amazed that the words stay still on the page instead of moving on a screen.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
The story opens with Margie's diary entry dated **17 May 2157**: Tommy has found a **real book**. Their grandparents' grandparents had told of a time when all stories were printed on paper. Children of 2157 read only on screens.

The book is about **school** — the old kind, centuries ago. Margie hates school. Her **mechanical teacher** has been giving her test after test in **geography**, and she has been doing worse and worse. Her mother called the **County Inspector**, a little man who took the teacher apart, found the geography sector was 'geared a little too quick', and slowed it to an average ten-year level.

Tommy explains that in old days the teacher was a **man**, all the children of the neighbourhood went to a **special building**, learned the same things, and helped each other. Margie's own school is a room next to her bedroom; the teacher switches on at the same time every day except Saturday and Sunday. As her teacher begins an arithmetic lesson on adding proper fractions, Margie dreams of the old schools — of children laughing and shouting together on the way home — and thinks about **the fun they had**.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **Margie** (11): bored and unhappy with her mechanical teacher; curious, imaginative; longs for company.
- **Tommy** (13): a little superior, knowledgeable, teases Margie; finds the book.
- **The mechanical teacher**: large, black and ugly, with a big screen for lessons and questions and a **slot** where homework and tests are inserted, written in a **punch code**.
- **The County Inspector**: a round little man who repairs and adjusts the teacher.
- **Margie's mother**: believes in the mechanical teacher; insists on regular lessons.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What kind of book did Tommy find? (2 marks)**
A very old printed book about school, with yellow, crinkly pages. Its words stood still instead of moving on a screen, which amazed the children.

**Q2. Why did Margie hate school? (3 marks)**
- Her mechanical teacher kept giving her tests in geography, and she did badly.
- She had to study alone in a room at home with no friends.
- Learning was fixed, mechanical and joyless.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Margie is **11**, Tommy **13** — not the other way round.
- The diary date is **17 May 2157** (future), not 1957.
- The subject she struggled with was **geography**; arithmetic was the lesson at the end.

activity.prompt: Put the events in order
items: Tommy finds a real book in the attic
Margie writes about it in her diary
Margie recalls the County Inspector fixing her teacher
Tommy explains that old teachers were men and schools were buildings
The mechanical teacher starts an arithmetic lesson
Margie dreams about the fun children had in old schools

quiz.q: In which year is the story set?
quiz.why: Margie's diary is dated 17 May 2157, so the story is set in the year 2157. The other years are not in the text.
Margie is eleven years old, and Tommy is thirteen. This age detail is given in the story.

quiz.q: Which subject was Margie doing poorly in?
quiz.why: Margie was doing badly in geography, and the mechanical teacher gave her test after test. Her mother then called the County Inspector.

quiz.q: What did the County Inspector do?
quiz.why: The County Inspector slowed down the geography sector of the mechanical teacher to an average ten-year level. He did not replace the teacher or close the school.

quiz.q: Homework was inserted into the teacher through:
quiz.why: Homework was put into a slot in the mechanical teacher, written in a punch code. The teacher then marked it at once.

scenes.text: During lockdown, Ishita attends class alone on a laptop for months.
When school reopens, she understands Margie: learning is better with friends around.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Technology vs human touch**: the mechanical teacher is efficient but cannot laugh, encourage or share.
- **Loneliness of individualised learning**: Margie learns alone; old schools gave **companionship**.
- **Grass is greener on the other side**: Margie romanticises old schools without knowing their problems.
- **Irony**: we, the readers, see old schools as normal; the future children see them as fun and strange.
- Asimov wrote this in **1951** as a prediction — today's online learning makes it feel real.

steps.title: Old school vs Margie's school
steps.body:
| Old school | Margie's school |
- Human teacher → mechanical teacher
- Special building → room at home
- Children learn together → child learns alone
- Same subjects for same age → adjusted to each child's mind
- Books on paper → screens
- Fun, friends, play → fixed timings, boredom

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **crinkly**: wrinkled
- **scornful(ly)**: showing contempt
- **loftily**: in a superior, proud way
- **dispute**: argue against
- **sorrowfully**: sadly
- **nonchalantly**: in a calm, casual, unconcerned way
- **geared**: set or adjusted (like a machine's gears)
- **sector**: a part or section (here, of the teacher's program)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Don't say the story *rejects* technology entirely — it shows its **limits**.
- 'Loftily' means **proudly**, not 'loudly'.

activity.prompt: Match the word to its meaning

quiz.q: A key theme of the story is:
options: Technology vs human touch in learning
quiz.why: The story sets technology against the human touch in learning. Margie's mechanical teacher is contrasted with the old human teachers and school.

quiz.q: What does Margie think the old-school children had?
quiz.why: Margie thinks that children in old schools had fun and companionship, learning with other children. She is envious of that togetherness.
'Loftily' means in a superior manner, as if one is better than the other. Tommy speaks in this way to Margie.
Margie's school was a room next to her bedroom, where the mechanical teacher was kept. So she studied at home and alone.

quiz.q: The story is an example of:
quiz.why: The story is set in the future and has machines like the mechanical teacher, so it is science fiction. It is not a fable or a biography.

lessons.title: Answer writing: short and long answers

scenes.text: Karan writes only one line for a 3-mark question and gets 1 mark.
His teacher shows him the PEE method: Point, Evidence, Explain.

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body:
- **2-3 marks (30–40 words)**: answer the question in the first line, then add 1–2 supporting details from the text.
- **5-6 marks (100–120 words)**: introduction (1 line) → 3–4 points with textual evidence → conclusion linking to the theme.
- Use your own words; quote only short phrases if needed.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. 'The mechanical teacher can never replace a human teacher.' Discuss with reference to the story. (6 marks)**
Asimov's story shows both the power and the limits of machine teaching.
- The mechanical teacher is efficient: it can be adjusted to each child's level, as the Inspector did for Margie.
- But it has no feelings; it cannot notice why Margie is unhappy or encourage her.
- Margie learns alone, with no friends to laugh with or help.
- Tommy's description of old schools, where children learned together from a human teacher, makes Margie long for that warmth.
Thus, technology can support learning, but the care, humour and companionship of a human teacher cannot be replaced.

steps.title: Solved short answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What did Margie's mother think about her school? (2 marks)** She believed the mechanical teacher was good; she called the Inspector when Margie did badly and insisted on regular lessons.

**Q2. Why did Tommy say the old teacher was a man? (2 marks)** In the old book, teachers were real people who taught groups of children in a school building, unlike their machine teachers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Retelling the whole story instead of answering the question.
- Writing opinions without evidence from the text.
- Exceeding the word limit badly — examiners value focus.

activity.prompt: Complete the summary
activity.text: Margie and Tommy found an old ___ about school. Margie's teacher was a ___ teacher, and an Inspector slowed its ___ sector.

quiz.q: For a 6-mark answer you should write about:
quiz.why: For a 6-mark answer, the board expects about 100 to 120 words. One sentence is too short and 500 words is too long.
PEE stands for Point, Evidence, Explain, a structure for analytical answers. You make a point, back it with evidence and explain it.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest evidence that Margie was lonely?
options: She studied alone in a room at home
quiz.why: Studying alone in a room at home, with no classmates, is the strongest evidence of Margie's loneliness. The other options are not related.

quiz.q: Why did Margie's mother call the Inspector?
options: Margie did badly in geography tests
quiz.why: Margie's mother called the Inspector because Margie kept doing badly in her geography tests. She wanted the machine fixed.
An answer should begin by directly answering the question. Copying the question or writing a title wastes time.

lessons.title: Extract-based questions and beyond the text

scenes.text: Students are asked to design a school for 2157.
Most designs mix smart screens with playgrounds and human teachers. They learned from Margie.

steps.title: Solved extract (paraphrased passage)
steps.body:
**Passage (paraphrased):** Margie's teacher was large, black and ugly, with a huge screen on which lessons were shown and questions asked. Worst of all was the slot where she had to put homework and test papers.
(a) What colour was the teacher? → Black.
(b) What did Margie dislike most? → The slot for homework and test papers.
(c) Find a word meaning 'unattractive'. → Ugly.
(d) What does this show about Margie's feelings? → She dislikes her mechanical, joyless school.

steps.title: Link to today
steps.body: AI tutors and online classes can personalise learning — just like Margie's teacher adjusted to her level. But students often report missing friends and teachers. Balanced 'blended learning' uses both.

steps.title: Writing link: diary entry
steps.body: Imagine you are Margie. Write a diary entry (100–120 words) about the day Tommy found the book. Format: date, day, time at top; first person; feelings; sign off with your name.

steps.title: Common mistakes in extracts
steps.body:
- Answer in a **full sentence** unless the question asks for a word.
- For 'find a word' questions, give the **exact** word from the passage in the same form.

activity.prompt: Would you prefer Margie's school or yours? Write three reasons.
activity.hint: Think of friends, teachers, flexibility, fun, pace of learning.

quiz.q: In the extract, which part did Margie hate most?
quiz.why: In the extract, Margie hated the slot most, the place where she had to put her homework and tests. The slot stood for the machine's cold routine.

quiz.q: A diary entry is written in:
quiz.why: A diary entry is written in the first person, since it records the writer's own thoughts and experiences. Second and third person do not suit it.

options: Mix of technology and in-person teaching
quiz.why: Blended learning is a mix of technology and in-person teaching. It is neither fully online nor without teachers.
'Ugly' means unattractive, not pleasant to look at. It is not a word for loud, kind or beautiful.
Isaac Asimov, the science fiction writer, wrote 'The Fun They Had'. The others are different writers.

questions.q: The author of 'The Fun They Had' is:
questions.why: 'The Fun They Had' was written by Isaac Asimov, a famous science fiction writer. R.K. Laxman, Basheer and Vikram Seth wrote other works.

questions.q: Who found the book?
questions.why: Tommy found the old printed book in the attic. He then showed it to Margie.

questions.q: Margie's teacher was:
questions.why: Margie's teacher was a mechanical machine, with a large screen and a slot. It was not a human being.

questions.q: Margie's school-room was:
questions.why: Margie's school-room was next to her bedroom, so she studied at home. It was not in a big building.

questions.q: The book's pages were:
questions.why: The old book's pages were yellow and crinkly, as they were very old. This shows how old printed books looked to the children of 2157.

questions.q: When did the teacher not work?
questions.why: The mechanical teacher worked every day except Saturdays and Sundays. Lessons ran on weekdays only.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Margie disliked her school. Reason (R): She studied alone with a mechanical teacher and kept failing geography tests.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Margie disliked her school because she studied alone with a mechanical teacher and kept failing geography tests.

questions.q: What was the arithmetic lesson about?
questions.why: The arithmetic lesson was about adding proper fractions. That is what the mechanical teacher was teaching in the story.

questions.q: Tommy's attitude towards Margie is mostly:
questions.why: Tommy speaks to Margie in a superior, teasing way. He acts like he knows more than she does.

questions.q: The County Inspector adjusted the geography sector to:
questions.why: The County Inspector adjusted the geography sector to an average ten-year level, as Margie was eleven and was faring poorly. He did not set it to zero.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the irony of the story?
options: Children of the future find our ordinary schools wonderful
questions.why: The irony is that children of the future find our ordinary schools wonderful, while we see them as normal. What is usual to us is fun for them.

questions.q: Case: A student says AI tutors will make schools unnecessary. Using the story, the best response is:
options: Technology can personalise learning but cannot replace human companionship and care
questions.why: The story shows that technology can personalise learning, but it cannot replace human companionship and care. A balanced reply is best.

questions.q: If Margie was 11 in 2157, in which year was she born?
questions.why: If Margie was 11 in 2157, she was born in 2157 − 11 = 2146. The other years do not fit.

questions.q: Which word best describes Margie at the end?
questions.why: At the end Margie is wistful and dreamy, thinking about the old schools and the fun the children had. She is not angry or frightened.

questions.q: Why did Margie's mother believe in the mechanical teacher?
options: She thought individually adjusted lessons were best for each child
questions.why: Her mother believed that lessons adjusted to each child's mind were best for them. She trusted the mechanical teacher for that reason.

courses.title: Ch 2 · The Sound of Music
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Two biographical pieces: Evelyn Glennie, the deaf Scottish percussionist who 'hears' through her body, and Ustad Bismillah Khan, who made the shehnai a classical instrument.
outcomes: Learners can narrate key events in the lives of Evelyn Glennie and Bismillah Khan
Learners can explain how determination overcomes disability
Learners can describe the history of the shehnai
Learners can write character sketches and answer board questions

lessons.title: Part I: Evelyn Glennie listens without hearing

scenes.text: A teacher tunes two drums to different notes and asks a deaf girl to put her hands on them.
She feels one note in her upper body and the other lower down. Music opens up to her.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Evelyn Glennie** is a world-famous Scottish percussionist who is profoundly deaf. Her hearing loss began gradually; when she was about **eight**, her mother noticed she did not respond when called. By **eleven** her marks had fallen and a specialist found she was **profoundly deaf**; she was advised to wear hearing aids and go to a school for the deaf.

Evelyn refused to give up. She was drawn to a girl playing a xylophone and wanted to play too. A percussionist, **Ron Forbes**, spotted her potential: he tuned two drums to different notes and taught her to feel the vibrations — one in her upper body, the other below the waist. She learned to sense sound through different parts of her body, and to play barefoot on wooden stages so she could feel the vibrations.

She joined the **Royal Academy of Music** in London (scoring among the highest marks in its history), became a soloist and has mastered around a thousand percussion instruments. She gives free concerts in prisons and hospitals and gives priority to classes for young musicians. She is an inspiration to deaf children and to everyone who faces obstacles.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- Scottish; profoundly deaf by 11.
- Teacher: **Ron Forbes**.
- Studied at the **Royal Academy of Music**, London.
- Feels music through **body vibrations**; performs barefoot.
- Free concerts in **prisons and hospitals**; supports young musicians.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Ron Forbes help Evelyn? (3 marks)** He tuned two drums to different notes and asked her to sense them through her body, not her ears; she discovered she could feel high notes in her upper body and low notes lower down. This opened the way to her career.

**Q2. How does Evelyn 'hear' music? (2 marks)** Through vibrations felt in different parts of her body — face, neck, arms, legs and bare feet on the stage floor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Evelyn was not born deaf; hearing loss was **gradual**, noticed around eight.
- She is **Scottish**, and studied in **London**.
- Ron Forbes was a percussionist teacher, not a doctor.

activity.prompt: Order the events of Evelyn's life

events.text: Mother notices she does not respond to her name
Found to be profoundly deaf; advised hearing aids
Ron Forbes teaches her to feel notes on drums
Joins the Royal Academy of Music, London
World-famous soloist; free concerts in prisons and hospitals

quiz.why: Evelyn Glennie is Scottish, born in Scotland. She is a famous percussionist.
Ron Forbes spotted Evelyn's potential and taught her to feel the sound as vibrations. He became her mentor.

options: To feel vibrations through the floor
quiz.why: Evelyn is deaf and performs barefoot so that she can feel the vibrations of the music through the floor. This helps her sense the sounds.
Evelyn studied at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It is a famous music school.

quiz.q: By what age was she found profoundly deaf?
quiz.why: By the age of eleven Evelyn was found to be profoundly deaf. She did not stop her music.

lessons.title: Part II: The shehnai of Bismillah Khan

scenes.text: Long ago, a ruler banned the shrill pungi in his palace. A barber decided to improve it.
He made a longer, broader pipe with seven holes. Its sweet sound was named the shehnai.

steps.title: History of the shehnai
steps.body: Emperor **Aurangzeb** banned the playing of the **pungi** in the royal residence because its sound was shrill and unpleasant. A **barber** (nai) from a family of professional musicians took a pipe with a natural hollow stem, longer and broader than the pungi, and made **seven holes** on it. When he played it, it produced soft, melodious sounds. He played before royalty; because it was first played in the **Shah's chambers** by a **nai**, it was called the **shehnai**. It was traditionally played in temples and at weddings and was part of the **naubat** (traditional ensemble at royal courts). Bismillah Khan brought it onto the classical stage.

steps.title: Bismillah Khan's life
steps.body:
- Born in **1916** at **Dumraon** in **Bihar**, in a family of musicians.
- Learned from his maternal uncle **Ali Bux**, who played the shehnai at the **Vishnu temple** in **Benaras**; young Bismillah practised on the banks of the **Ganga** and found inspiration in its flow.
- First break in **1938** with the opening of **All India Radio, Lucknow**.
- On **15 August 1947**, he played the shehnai from the **Red Fort** to welcome India's Independence (raag Kafi), with Pandit Nehru present.
- First Indian invited to perform at the **Lincoln Center Hall** in the USA; performed at Montreal's World Exposition, the Cannes Art Festival and the Osaka Trade Fair. An auditorium in **Tehran** was named after him.
- Music in films: Vijay Bhatt's *Gunj Uthi Shehnai*; also a Kannada film *Sanadi Apanna*.
- Awards: Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan and **Bharat Ratna (2001)**.
- He refused offers to settle in the USA — he could not leave Benaras, Dumraon and the Ganga.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did the shehnai get its name? (2 marks)** It was first played in the Shah's chambers by a nai (barber): 'shah' + 'nai' → shehnai.

**Q2. Why did Bismillah Khan refuse to settle in the USA? (3 marks)** He was deeply attached to Benaras and Dumraon, the Ganga and the temple where he learned music; he felt his music came from his roots in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The ban was on the **pungi** (not the shehnai) by **Aurangzeb**.
- Born in **Dumraon, Bihar**; trained in **Benaras**.
- Bharat Ratna in **2001**.

activity.prompt: Match the fact to Bismillah Khan's life
pairs: All India Radio, Lucknow — first break

quiz.why: Emperor Aurangzeb banned the pungi, because its sound was shrill and unpleasant to the ear. Shah Jahan, Akbar and Babur did not.

quiz.q: How many holes did the barber make in the new instrument?
quiz.why: The barber made seven holes in a hollow stem of reed, creating a new instrument, the shehnai. He did so from a pungi with a smoother sound.

quiz.q: Bismillah Khan's uncle played at the:
quiz.why: Bismillah Khan's uncle played the shehnai at the Vishnu temple in Benaras. The young Bismillah learned from him.

quiz.q: He was the first Indian to perform at:
quiz.why: Bismillah Khan was the first Indian to be invited to perform at the Lincoln Center Hall in the USA. It was a major honour.

quiz.q: He received the Bharat Ratna in:
quiz.why: Bismillah Khan received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, in 2001. It was not in 1947 or 1991.

scenes.text: Rohit, who stammers, is afraid to join the debate club.
After reading about Evelyn and Bismillah Khan, he signs up: 'If they found a way, so can I.'

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Determination and hard work** overcome obstacles (Evelyn's deafness).
- **Passion and dedication** to an art.
- **Roots and identity** — Bismillah Khan's love for Benaras and the Ganga.
- **Music as a universal language** that unites people.
- **Giving back** — Evelyn's free concerts; Bismillah Khan's lifelong commitment to the shehnai.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **percussionist**: musician who plays instruments like drums
- **profoundly deaf**: completely or almost completely deaf
- **reverberation**: echo, repeated sound
- **ensemble**: a group of musicians
- **gruelling**: very tiring, demanding
- **auspicious**: promising good luck
- **maestro**: a master of an art
- **mesmerised**: spellbound

steps.title: Solved character sketches
steps.body:
**Evelyn Glennie (6 marks)**: determined — refused to give up after deafness; hardworking — practised long hours; sensitive — learned to feel sound through her body; generous — free concerts for prisoners and patients; inspiring — role model for disabled people.

**Bismillah Khan (6 marks)**: devoted to his art; humble despite fame; deeply rooted in Indian culture (Ganga, Benaras); secular — Muslim musician playing at a Hindu temple; patriotic — played at the Red Fort in 1947, refused to settle abroad.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A character sketch needs **traits + evidence**, not a summary.
- Don't write 'Evelyn was born deaf'.

activity.prompt: Which musician does this describe?

items.text: Practised on the banks of the Ganga
Played at the Red Fort in 1947
Mastered about a thousand percussion instruments
Refused to settle in the USA

quiz.why: A percussionist plays drums and similar instruments that are struck, such as the xylophone. Piano, flute and violin are not percussion instruments.
'Maestro' means a master of an art, especially a great musician. It does not mean a beginner.

quiz.q: Which trait best fits Bismillah Khan?
quiz.why: Bismillah Khan was deeply rooted in his culture, loving Benaras and the Ganga. He refused to move abroad.

quiz.q: Which theme is common to both parts?
quiz.why: Both parts are about people deeply devoted to music, Evelyn and Bismillah Khan. This is the shared theme.
'Gruelling' means very tiring or exhausting. It is the opposite of easy.

scenes.text: Students must write an imaginary interview with Bismillah Khan for the school magazine.
Aditi prepares five questions — about the Ganga, the Red Fort and why he never left India.

steps.title: Solved extract (paraphrased)
steps.body:
**Passage (paraphrased):** Evelyn learned to open her mind and body to sounds and vibrations. Ron Forbes made her feel the notes, and she discovered she could sense higher drums from the waist up and lower ones from the waist down.
(a) Who helped Evelyn? → Ron Forbes.
(b) Where did she feel the higher notes? → In her upper body (above the waist).
(c) What does 'vibrations' mean here? → Tiny shaking movements produced by sound.
(d) Which quality of Evelyn is shown? → Openness and determination to learn.

steps.title: Writing link: biographical sketch
steps.body: Write a 120-word biographical sketch of Bismillah Khan using these notes: born 1916 Dumraon · learned from Ali Bux, Benaras · AIR Lucknow 1938 · Red Fort 1947 · Lincoln Center · Bharat Ratna 2001 · loved the Ganga. Use past tense, link with 'Later', 'In 1947', 'Despite…'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In biographical sketches, keep a **chronological** order.
- Avoid bullet points in the final answer — write a paragraph.

steps.title: Disability and inclusion
steps.body: India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 promotes inclusive education. Evelyn's story shows what support and belief can unlock.

statements.s: Bismillah Khan played the shehnai at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947.
Evelyn was advised to go to a school for the deaf.
statements.why: But she chose a normal school path.

statements.s: The shehnai was invented by a court musician called Ali Bux.
statements.why: A barber improved the pungi; Ali Bux was Bismillah's uncle.

statements.s: A biographical sketch should follow chronological order.

quiz.q: In the extract, higher notes were felt:
quiz.why: In the extract, Evelyn felt higher notes in the upper body, above the waist, and lower notes in the legs and feet. She trained herself to feel them.

quiz.q: A biographical sketch is written mainly in:
quiz.why: A biographical sketch tells of a person's life, which has already happened, so it is mainly in the past tense. It is not written in the imperative.
Evelyn's teacher was Ron Forbes, who taught her percussion. The others are not her teacher.
Evelyn never gave up in spite of her deafness, so determined suits her best. Lazy, careless or arrogant do not.

quiz.q: Bismillah Khan's first break came with:
quiz.why: Bismillah Khan's first break came with All India Radio, Lucknow, in 1938. It made him known to many.

questions.q: Evelyn Glennie plays:
questions.why: Evelyn Glennie is a percussionist. She plays drums and similar instruments, not the guitar, sitar or shehnai.

questions.q: Bismillah Khan was born in:
questions.why: Bismillah Khan was born in Dumraon, in Bihar. He later lived in Benaras.

questions.q: The shehnai developed from the:
questions.why: The shehnai developed from the pungi, which had been banned. A barber improved it by making seven holes.

questions.q: Who was Evelyn's mentor?
questions.why: Ron Forbes was Evelyn's mentor, who showed her how to feel sound. The others are not linked to her.

questions.q: Bismillah Khan's music was used in the film:
questions.why: Bismillah Khan's shehnai was used in Vijay Bhatt's film Gunj Uthi Shehnai. It is not in the other films.

questions.q: Evelyn gives free concerts in:
questions.why: Evelyn gives free concerts in prisons and hospitals, for people who cannot easily attend music programmes. This shows her kindness.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Evelyn performs barefoot. Reason (R): She senses sound through vibrations in the floor.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Evelyn performs barefoot because she senses the sound through vibrations in the floor.

questions.q: Why was the pungi banned?
options: Its sound was shrill and unpleasant
questions.why: The pungi was banned because its sound was shrill and unpleasant. It was not foreign, costly or religious.

questions.q: Which statement about Bismillah Khan is FALSE?
options: He played at the Red Fort in 1947
questions.why: Bismillah Khan refused to settle in the USA because he loved Benaras and the Ganga, so that statement is false. The other statements are true.

questions.q: The shehnai was traditionally part of the:
questions.why: The shehnai was traditionally played in the naubat, the ensemble at royal courts and temples. It was not part of a choir or band.

questions.q: Bismillah Khan was born in 1916 and got the Bharat Ratna in 2001. How old was he then?
questions.why: Age = 2001 − 1916 = 85 years. The other values do not match.

questions.q: Case: A deaf student is told music is not for her. Which line of thought from the chapter would help most?
options: Like Evelyn, explore other ways to sense and learn, with the right mentor
questions.why: Like Evelyn, a deaf student can explore other ways of sensing sound and learning, with a good mentor. Giving up or accepting limits is not the lesson.

questions.q: What does Bismillah Khan's playing at a Vishnu temple show?
questions.why: Playing at a Vishnu temple, though he was Muslim, shows the shared, syncretic culture of India. Music goes beyond religion.

questions.q: Which pair of traits is common to both musicians?
questions.why: Both musicians were dedicated to their art and humble about their success. Arrogance and laziness do not describe them.

questions.q: The title 'The Sound of Music' is apt because:
options: Both parts are about musicians who found unique ways to create or experience music
questions.why: Both parts are about musicians who found unusual ways to create or experience music, so the title suits. It is not about a film, noise or radio.

courses.title: Ch 3 · The Little Girl
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Katherine Mansfield's story of Kezia, a girl afraid of her stern father, and the night she discovers his gentle side.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story and the pincushion incident
Learners can trace the change in Kezia's attitude towards her father
Learners can discuss parent–child relationships
Learners can answer board-style questions with evidence

scenes.text: Every morning Kezia waits for her father's footsteps to leave the house. Only then does she feel she can breathe.
One stormy night, alone and frightened, she discovers a side of him she never knew.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Kezia** is scared of her father. Every morning before he leaves for work he comes to her room and gives her a casual kiss; she feels relieved when he goes. In the evening his return makes her nervous; she **stutters** when she speaks to him. He seems huge and stern — his hands, neck and especially his mouth when he yawns.

On Sundays her **grandmother** sends her to the drawing room to 'have a nice talk' with her parents, but her father finds fault with her. For his birthday, grandmother suggests she make a **pin-cushion**. Kezia finds some papers on her mother's table, tears them up and stuffs the cushion — but they were her father's **important speech** for the Port Authority. He is furious and punishes her by **hitting her hands with a ruler**. She cries and wonders why God made fathers.

She watches the **Macdonalds** next door: their father plays and laughs with his many children, which surprises her.

One night, her mother falls ill and is taken to the hospital with grandmother; Kezia is left with Alice the cook. She has a **nightmare** of a butcher with a knife and a rope. Her father comes, takes her into his own bed, and comforts her. As he falls asleep, tired, she realises he works hard and is too tired to play. She feels sympathy for him: he is not so big after all, and has a heart.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **Kezia**: timid, sensitive, imaginative, afraid of her father; finally understanding.
- **Father**: stern, strict, short-tempered, hardworking; caring underneath.
- **Mother**: frail, mostly passive.
- **Grandmother**: loving, gentle, protective; Kezia's comfort.
- **Mr Macdonald**: a jolly father who plays with his children — a contrast.
- **Alice**: the cook, unkind to Kezia.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did Kezia stutter before her father? (2 marks)** She was so frightened of his stern looks and fault-finding that she became nervous and could not speak normally.

**Q2. Describe the pin-cushion incident. (3 marks)** For her father's birthday, Kezia made a pin-cushion and stuffed it with papers she found — actually his important speech for the Port Authority. When he found out, he punished her by striking her palms with a ruler.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The papers were her father's **speech** for the **Port Authority**, not his bank papers.
- She was comforted by her **father** during the nightmare, not grandmother (who was away).
- The Macdonalds are **neighbours**, not relatives.

activity.prompt: Order the events
items: Kezia feels relief when her father leaves each morning
Grandmother suggests a pin-cushion for father's birthday
Kezia stuffs it with father's speech papers
Father punishes her with a ruler
Kezia watches the playful Macdonald family
Kezia has a nightmare; father comforts her
Kezia realises her father has a big heart

quiz.why: Kezia was afraid of her father, who seemed stern and frightening to her. She was not afraid of her mother or grandmother.

quiz.q: What did Kezia make for her father's birthday?
quiz.why: Kezia made a pin-cushion for her father's birthday, on her grandmother's suggestion. She stuffed it with her own hair.

options: His speech for the Port Authority
quiz.why: The papers were her father's speech for the Port Authority. Kezia tore them up by mistake while making the pin-cushion.

quiz.q: Who comforted Kezia after her nightmare?
quiz.why: Her father comforted Kezia after her nightmare, which surprised her. It showed his caring side.

options: A butcher with a knife and rope
quiz.why: Kezia dreamed about a butcher with a knife and a rope. It frightened her, and she woke up screaming.

scenes.text: Nisha's mother works late and is often too tired to talk.
One night Nisha finds her mother asleep over office files and covers her with a shawl — she understands.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Parent–child relationship and communication gap**.
- **Fear vs love**: strict discipline can hide care.
- **Growing understanding**: Kezia moves from fear to empathy.
- **Contrast** between Kezia's father and Mr Macdonald shows different parenting styles.
- **Hard work and fatigue** of the breadwinner.

steps.title: Change in Kezia's attitude
steps.body:
1. Fear — she dreads his presence.
2. Resentment — after the ruler punishment, she wonders why God made fathers.
3. Envy/curiosity — seeing Mr Macdonald play with his children.
4. Understanding — during the night, she feels his warmth and sees his tiredness.
5. Empathy and love — 'Poor father' feeling: he is not so big, and needs care too.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **stutter**: speak with repeated sounds due to nervousness
- **timid**: shy, easily frightened
- **punish/punishment**
- **solemnly**: seriously
- **sympathy**: sharing someone's feelings of sorrow
- **frail**: weak, delicate

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Don't call the father 'cruel' without nuance — the story shows he is strict but caring.
- The change in Kezia happens gradually, not suddenly at the pin-cushion.

statements.s: Mr Macdonald played happily with his children.
Kezia's attitude to her father never changes.
statements.why: She moves from fear to empathy.

statements.s: Her father was tired because he worked hard.
The story is about a girl and her grandmother's quarrel.
statements.why: It is about Kezia and her father.

quiz.why: The main theme is the parent-child relationship, between Kezia and her father. It shows how a child misjudges a strict parent.
'Timid' means shy and easily frightened. Kezia is timid in front of her father.

quiz.q: Mr Macdonald's role in the story is to:
quiz.why: Mr Macdonald is a playful father, in contrast to Kezia's strict one. He shows what a warm relationship could be.
At the end Kezia feels sympathy and love for her father, because she understands how tired he is. Her earlier fear gives way.
'Frail' means weak and delicate. It is the opposite of strong.

scenes.text: In class debate, half say the father is a villain, half say he is misunderstood.
The teacher asks them to write answers with evidence from the text, not just opinions.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. How does Kezia's view of her father change? (6 marks)**
At first Kezia sees her father as a frightening giant. She waits for him to leave, stutters before him and feels he only finds fault. The ruler punishment after the pin-cushion incident deepens her fear. Watching Mr Macdonald play with his children, she wonders why her father is different. Then, on the night of her nightmare, her father takes her into his bed and comforts her. Feeling his warmth and seeing him fall asleep from tiredness, she realises he works hard and has no energy for play. Her fear turns into empathy; she sees he has a big heart.

steps.title: Solved character sketch: the father
steps.body: Strict and short-tempered (punishes with a ruler) · hardworking (too tired to play) · conventional view of discipline · loving at heart (comforts Kezia, lets her sleep beside him) · represents many parents who show love through providing rather than playing.

steps.title: Value-based answer
steps.body: Questions like 'What should parents learn from this story?' need 3 points: communicate, show affection openly, understand children's fears — plus one line linking to the story.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the father's punishment (**ruler on palms**) with other details.
- Using quotation marks for long lines — paraphrase.

activity.prompt: Father's trait: harsh side or caring side?

items.text: Takes her into his bed after the nightmare
Finds fault with her on Sundays
Works hard to support the family
Gently comforts her and tells her to sleep

quiz.q: Which incident shows the father's caring side?
quiz.why: Comforting Kezia after her nightmare shows his caring side. Scolding, the ruler punishment and reading the paper show a stern side.
A character sketch needs traits of the character, supported by evidence from the text. A mere summary or a drawing is not enough.

quiz.q: The father was too tired to play because:
quiz.why: The father was too tired to play because he worked hard all day. It was not that he disliked children or was lazy.
Grandmother suggested the pin-cushion as a gift for Kezia's father. Kezia then made it.

options: Lessons with a link to the story
quiz.why: A value-based answer should state the lessons and link them to the story. Only a title or grammar rules are not enough.

scenes.text: Kezia, now grown up, writes a letter to her father remembering that stormy night.
She thanks him for the moment she finally saw his heart.

steps.title: Solved extract (paraphrased)
steps.body:
**Passage (paraphrased):** Kezia lay beside her father, his arm around her. He fell asleep quickly, worn out. She thought how hard he worked and how he was too tired to play.
(a) Where is Kezia? → In her father's bed.
(b) Why did he fall asleep quickly? → He was tired after working hard.
(c) What new feeling does Kezia have? → Sympathy/understanding.
(d) Find a word meaning 'exhausted'. → 'Worn out'.

steps.title: Writing link: diary entry as Kezia
steps.body: Write Kezia's diary entry on the morning after the nightmare (100–120 words): date · what happened · how she felt · what she now understands about her father · a resolution (e.g., to talk to him more).

steps.title: Real-life link
steps.body: Many children fear strict parents. Talking about feelings, spending small moments together (a walk, a meal) and parents listening without judgment can close the gap. If a child is being harmed, a trusted adult or **Childline 1098** can help.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In a diary entry, avoid writing it like a letter ('Dear…' is optional for diary; no address).
- Keep the tone personal and reflective.

activity.prompt: Recall a time you misunderstood someone in your family. What helped you see their side?
activity.hint: Think of a moment of tiredness, hidden effort or a kind act you noticed later.

quiz.q: In the extract, Kezia's feeling is:
quiz.why: In the extract, Kezia feels sympathy, because she understands her father's tiredness. She no longer fears him.
'Worn out' means exhausted, very tired. It does not mean bored, excited or torn.
A diary entry should be personal and reflective, as it records one's own thoughts and feelings. It is not formal or in the third person.
Katherine Mansfield wrote 'The Little Girl'. Oscar Wilde, Ruskin Bond and O. Henry wrote other works.

quiz.q: Which helpline helps children in India?
quiz.why: Childline, 1098, is the helpline for children in India. 100 is for police and 108 for ambulances.

questions.q: The author of 'The Little Girl':
questions.why: 'The Little Girl' was written by Katherine Mansfield. Isaac Asimov, Vikram Seth and Chekhov wrote different works.

questions.q: The little girl's name is:
questions.why: The little girl's name is Kezia. Margie is from a different story.

questions.q: Kezia stuttered in front of:
questions.why: Kezia stuttered in front of her father because she was afraid of him. This shows her fear.

questions.q: The father's speech was for the:
questions.why: The father's speech was for the Port Authority. Kezia accidentally tore it to make the pin-cushion.

questions.q: How did the father punish Kezia?
options: Struck her palms with a ruler
questions.why: The father punished Kezia by striking her palms with a ruler. This hurt her and added to her fear.

questions.q: When was Kezia left with Alice?
options: When mother was taken to hospital with grandmother
questions.why: Kezia was left with Alice when her mother was taken to the hospital with grandmother. It was during this time that things changed.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Kezia felt relieved each morning. Reason (R): Her father left for office.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Kezia felt relieved each morning when her father left for the office, since his absence ended her fear.

questions.q: What does the Macdonald family represent?
questions.why: The Macdonald family shows a warm, playful father-child relationship, in contrast to Kezia's home. They are not strict or servants.

questions.q: Which word best describes grandmother?
questions.why: Grandmother is loving and protective, and comforts Kezia. She is not cruel or indifferent.

questions.q: Kezia's realisation at the end is that her father:
options: Is hardworking, tired, and has a big heart
questions.why: Kezia realises that her father is hardworking, tired, and has a big heart. She stops fearing him.

questions.q: Which sequence of Kezia's feelings is correct?
questions.why: Kezia's feelings change from fear to resentment, then envy of the Macdonald children, and finally empathy for her father. This is the gradual change.

questions.q: Case: A father scolds his son for low marks but stays up all night when the son is ill. This mirrors which part of the story?
options: The father's hidden care shown in the nightmare scene
questions.why: A father who scolds but stays up all night mirrors the father in the nightmare scene, whose care was hidden beneath strictness. It shows the same hidden love.

questions.q: Why did the father's yawning mouth frighten Kezia?
options: It reminded her of a giant/ogre — showing a child's exaggerated fear
questions.why: Kezia saw her father's yawning mouth as that of a giant or ogre. This shows a child's exaggerated fear.

questions.q: The story is told mostly from whose perspective?
questions.why: The story is told mostly from Kezia's point of view, showing how the world looks to a child. It is not told by her father or Alice.

questions.q: What is the best lesson for parents in the story?
options: Show love openly and communicate; strictness can hide care that children can't see
questions.why: The lesson for parents is to show love openly and talk to children. Strictness can hide care that children cannot see.

courses.title: Ch 4 · A Truly Beautiful Mind
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: A biographical account of Albert Einstein — his childhood, schooling, patent-office years, the theory of relativity, the letter on the atom bomb and his work for peace.
outcomes: Learners can sequence the key events in Einstein's life
Learners can explain his contributions and his role in the atom bomb debate
Learners can describe his personality and values
Learners can answer board-style questions

scenes.text: Baby Albert's head seems too big; his mother worries. He starts talking late, at about two and a half.
At six he starts violin lessons, which he loves all his life.

steps.title: Early life (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Albert Einstein** was born on **14 March 1879** in **Ulm, Germany**. As a baby his head seemed large; he started talking late (about **two and a half**) and for a time repeated every sentence twice. His playmates called him 'Brother Boring'.

At **six** he began **violin** lessons; music stayed with him all his life. His family moved to **Munich**, where he went to school. He did well, especially in maths, but hated the **regimentation** and rote learning of his school (Luitpold Gymnasium) and clashed with teachers. At **15**, when his family moved to Milan, he left school.

He continued his studies in **Switzerland**, at the university (Federal Polytechnic) in **Zurich**, where he enjoyed the freedom of thought. There he met **Mileva Marić**, a fellow student, whom he later married.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did Einstein leave school in Munich? (2 marks)** He disliked its strict discipline and rote learning and clashed with teachers; he left at 15 when his family moved to Milan.

**Q2. Why did his playmates call him 'Brother Boring'? (2 marks)** He preferred tinkering and thinking alone to playing their games.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Born in **Ulm** (not Munich); schooled in **Munich**; university in **Zurich**.
- He was **good** at maths — the myth that he failed maths is false.

steps.title: Quick facts
steps.body: - 1879 born, Ulm · violin at 6 · Munich school · left at 15 · Zurich university · met Mileva Marić.

activity.prompt: Match the place to Einstein's life
pairs: Family moved; he left school at 15

quiz.why: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, in Germany, in 1879. He did not grow up there; the family moved to Munich.
Einstein started violin lessons at the age of six. He kept playing it all his life.

quiz.q: Why did he dislike his Munich school?
quiz.why: Einstein disliked his Munich school because of its regimentation and rote learning. He preferred to think for himself.

quiz.q: Where did he study at university?
quiz.why: Einstein studied at the university in Zurich. It is in Switzerland.

quiz.q: Whom did he meet at university?
quiz.why: At university in Zurich he met Mileva Marić, who became his first wife. She was a fellow student.

scenes.text: In Bern, a young technical expert checks other people's inventions by day.
In his spare time, he writes papers that will change physics forever.

steps.title: Career (in our own words)
steps.body:
After university Einstein could not get an academic job. He worked as a **technical expert** at the **patent office in Bern**, assessing other people's inventions; he secretly worked on his own ideas.

In **1905** he published a paper on the **special theory of relativity**, which showed that time and distance are not absolute. From it came the famous equation **E = mc²**, linking mass and energy.

In **1915** he published the **general theory of relativity**, a new explanation of gravity. In **1919** British astronomers observing a solar eclipse confirmed his prediction that light bends near the sun; newspapers hailed him and he became world famous. He received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** (for 1921).

He married Mileva in 1903; the marriage ended in divorce (1919), and he later married his cousin **Elsa**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What did Einstein do at the patent office? (2 marks)** As a technical expert, he examined inventions submitted for patents, while working on his own theories.

**Q2. How did Einstein become world famous? (3 marks)** His general theory of relativity (1915) predicted that light would bend around the sun; in 1919 British scientists confirmed this during a solar eclipse; newspapers spread the news, making him a celebrity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Special relativity = **1905**; general relativity = **1915**; eclipse confirmation = **1919**.
- E = mc² relates **mass and energy**, not speed and distance.

steps.title: In simple terms
steps.body: E = mc² means a small amount of mass can be turned into a huge amount of energy because c (speed of light) is very large. This idea underlies nuclear energy.

activity.prompt: Order Einstein's achievements

events.text: Joins the patent office in Bern
Special theory of relativity; E = mc²

quiz.q: Einstein worked at a patent office in:
quiz.why: Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern, Switzerland. He did his famous early work there.

quiz.q: The special theory of relativity was published in:
quiz.why: His special theory of relativity was published in 1905. 1915 was general relativity.
E = mc² links mass and energy, saying that they are equivalent. It does not link speed and time or force and area.

quiz.q: His prediction was confirmed in 1919 by observing a:
quiz.why: In 1919 a solar eclipse confirmed his prediction that light bends near the sun. This made him world famous.

quiz.q: He won the Nobel Prize in:
quiz.why: Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1921, for his work on the photoelectric effect. It was not in chemistry or peace.

lessons.title: The bomb, peace and Einstein's legacy

scenes.text: 1939. Fearing Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb, Einstein signs a letter warning the US President.
After Hiroshima and Nagasaki, he spends his last years urging the world to give up such weapons.

steps.title: Later life (in our own words)
steps.body:
When **Hitler** came to power in **1933**, Einstein, who was Jewish, emigrated to the **USA** (Princeton).

In **1939**, worried that Nazi Germany might develop an atomic bomb, he wrote a famous letter to US President **Franklin D. Roosevelt**, warning him of the danger and the possibility of a bomb of enormous power. This helped start American research into atomic weapons.

In **1945**, the US dropped atomic bombs on **Hiroshima and Nagasaki** in Japan. Einstein was deeply shocked. He wrote a public letter to the **United Nations**, proposing a **world government** to prevent such destruction. In his last years he worked for **peace and democracy** and against nuclear weapons.

He died in **1955**, aged **76**. He became a symbol of a brilliant, independent mind; a magazine later named him 'Person of the Century'.

steps.title: Einstein's personality
steps.body:
- Curious and independent thinker; disliked rote rules.
- Loved music (violin).
- Humble; simple lifestyle.
- Pacifist and humanitarian — worried about misuse of science.
- Courageous — spoke out against tyranny.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did Einstein write to Roosevelt? (2 marks)** To warn him that Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb, and to urge the US to act.

**Q2. How did Einstein react to the bombing of Hiroshima? (3 marks)** He was shocked and saddened; he wrote to the UN proposing a world government and campaigned for peace and against nuclear weapons for the rest of his life.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Einstein did **not** build the bomb; he wrote a warning letter.
- He died in **1955**, aged 76.

statements.s: Einstein emigrated to the USA after Hitler came to power.
Einstein personally designed the atomic bomb.
statements.why: He only wrote a warning letter.

statements.s: He proposed a world government after Hiroshima.
statements.why: In a letter to the UN.

statements.s: He died in 1975.

quiz.q: Einstein wrote to which US President?
quiz.why: In 1939 Einstein wrote to US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, warning about atomic weapons research. Kennedy, Truman and Lincoln were not in office then.

quiz.q: The atom bombs were dropped on:
quiz.why: The atom bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in Japan, in 1945. Einstein was deeply distressed.
After the bombings, Einstein proposed a world government to prevent war. He had become a strong pacifist.
Einstein died in 1955. 1933 was when he left Germany.

quiz.q: Which trait best describes his later years?
quiz.why: In his later years Einstein was a peace-lover who campaigned against war and nuclear weapons. He was not a warmonger.

lessons.title: Answer writing, vocabulary and writing link

scenes.text: A viral post says 'Einstein failed maths'. Arnav checks his textbook.
He finds Einstein was excellent at maths. He posts a correction with the facts.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **regimentation**: strict discipline, rigid control
- **freak**: an unusual person/thing (his mother's worry about his large head)
- **genius**: exceptional intellectual ability
- **pacifist**: one who opposes war
- **emigrate**: leave one's country to live in another
- **eclipse**: when one celestial body hides another

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. Why is Einstein called 'a truly beautiful mind'? (6 marks)**
Einstein's mind was beautiful not only for its brilliance but for its humanity. As a child he questioned rules and loved music. His special and general theories of relativity changed how we understand time, space and gravity. Yet he remained humble and simple. When he realised the danger of nuclear weapons, he warned the US President in 1939 and, after Hiroshima, appealed to the UN for a world government and worked for peace. His intellect, creativity and conscience together make him a truly beautiful mind.

steps.title: Writing link: diary/letter
steps.body: Write a letter (as Einstein) to a young student, encouraging curiosity over rote learning (120 words). Use informal letter format: address, date, salutation, body, closing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Don't fill answers with dates only — explain significance.
- 'Emigrate' (leave) vs 'immigrate' (come into).

activity.prompt: Match words and meanings
pairs: Leave one's country to live elsewhere

quiz.why: A pacifist is one who opposes war. It does not mean a soldier or a scientist.

options: Leave one's country to live elsewhere
quiz.why: To emigrate is to leave one's own country to live elsewhere. To immigrate is to come into a country.

options: No, he was very good at it
quiz.why: The idea that Einstein failed maths is a myth. He was very good at it from an early age.

quiz.q: The title 'A Truly Beautiful Mind' refers to his:
quiz.why: The title refers to his brilliance and his humanity, i.e. his great intellect and conscience. It is not about wealth or looks.

options: A friendly closing like 'With love' or 'Yours'
quiz.why: An informal letter ends with a friendly closing such as 'With love' or 'Yours'. 'Yours faithfully' is for formal letters.

questions.q: Einstein was born in:
questions.why: Einstein was born in 1879 in Ulm. 1905 was the year of his special relativity paper.

questions.q: He played the:
questions.why: Einstein played the violin, which he started learning at six. It remained a lifelong love.

questions.q: His first wife was:
questions.why: His first wife was Mileva Marić, whom he met at university. Elsa was his second wife.

questions.q: Where did he work as a technical expert?
questions.why: He worked as a technical expert at the patent office in Bern. He did not work at a bank or hospital.

questions.q: General relativity was published in:
questions.why: General relativity was published in 1915. Special relativity came in 1905 and the eclipse in 1919.

questions.q: Einstein moved to the USA because:
options: Hitler came to power and he was Jewish
questions.why: Einstein moved to the USA because Hitler had come to power and he was Jewish, so he was not safe in Germany. It was not just a job offer.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Einstein became world famous in 1919. Reason (R): An eclipse confirmed his prediction that light bends near the sun.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. In 1919 an eclipse confirmed that light bends near the sun, and the news made Einstein world famous.

questions.q: Why did Einstein leave school at 15?
options: Disliked regimentation; family moved to Milan
questions.why: Einstein left school at 15 because he disliked its regimentation, and his family had moved to Milan. He did not fail exams or join the army.

questions.q: Which is NOT true?
options: He won the Nobel Prize in Physics
questions.why: Einstein did not support nuclear war, so that statement is not true. He won the Nobel Prize, wrote to Roosevelt in 1939 and proposed a world government.

questions.q: E = mc² means:
options: Energy equals mass times the square of the speed of light
questions.why: E = mc² means energy equals mass times the square of the speed of light. It shows how mass and energy are equivalent.

questions.q: Einstein died in 1955. Born in 1879, how old was he?
questions.why: Age = 1955 − 1879 = 76 years. The other values would be off by one or more years.

questions.q: How many years passed between special relativity and its general form?
questions.why: Special relativity was published in 1905 and general relativity in 1915. The gap is 1915 − 1905 = 10 years.

questions.q: Case: A scientist discovers something that can be used for energy or weapons. What would Einstein's later life advise?
options: Sell it to the highest bidder
Use science responsibly, speak out against misuse, work for peace
questions.why: Einstein's later life shows that scientists should use science responsibly, speak out against misuse and work for peace. Hiding or selling it is not his example.

questions.q: Which best explains why he was called 'Brother Boring'?
options: He spoke slowly and preferred solitary thinking to games
questions.why: As a child Einstein spoke slowly and preferred solitary thinking to games, so he was called 'Brother Boring'. It was not about illness or unkindness.

questions.q: Which statement best shows the irony in Einstein's life?
options: A peace-lover's letter helped start atomic weapons research
questions.why: The irony is that Einstein, a lover of peace, wrote a letter that helped start atomic weapons research. The other facts are not ironic.

courses.title: Ch 5 · The Snake and the Mirror
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Vaikom Muhammad Basheer's humorous story of a vain young homeopath whose daydreams of wealth and marriage are interrupted when a snake coils around his arm.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story and its climax
Learners can identify humour, irony and the theme of vanity
Learners can describe the doctor's character
Learners can answer board-style questions

story.title: A hot night, a small room

scenes.text: A young doctor admires his face in a mirror and plans to shave every day and grow a moustache.
Suddenly something falls on his shoulder and coils round his arm — a snake!

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
The narrator, a **homeopath** who is poor and lives in a small rented room without electricity, tells his friends about a frightening experience.

One hot night he returns home, lights a kerosene lamp and hears a faint sound from the roof, which he assumes is a rat. Sitting before a **mirror**, he admires his face and decides he is handsome. He plans to **shave daily**, **grow a thin moustache** and always look smart. He even dreams of **marrying a rich, plump lady doctor** with a good practice, so that he can live comfortably.

Suddenly a **snake** falls from the rafters onto his shoulder and coils around his **left arm** above the elbow. He freezes 'like a stone image', holding his breath. His mind races; he prays to God. The snake's head is close to his face.

Then the snake turns its head and looks into the **mirror** — perhaps admiring its own reflection. The doctor slowly slips away, runs out of the room and calls his neighbours. When they return with a lamp, the snake has gone. The doctor drops his dream of marrying the fat lady doctor and of shaving daily — humbled by the experience.

steps.title: The narrator
steps.body:
- A young homeopath, poor (income was small) but vain about his looks.
- Imaginative; dreams big.
- Funny; laughs at himself.
- Becomes humble after facing death.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What were the doctor's two decisions while looking in the mirror? (2 marks)** To shave daily and grow a thin moustache to look handsome (and he dreamed of marrying a rich, plump lady doctor).

**Q2. How did the doctor escape? (3 marks)** He remained still, holding his breath; when the snake turned to look into the mirror, it uncoiled and moved towards it; he quietly slipped away and ran out of the room.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The snake coiled round his **left arm**, not his neck.
- The narrator is a **homeopath**, not an allopathic surgeon.
- He did **not** kill the snake.

activity.prompt: Order the events
items: The doctor returns to his room on a hot night
He hears a sound and thinks it is a rat
He admires himself in the mirror
He decides to shave daily and grow a moustache
A snake falls on his shoulder and coils round his arm
The snake looks into the mirror
The doctor escapes and calls neighbours

quiz.why: The narrator, the doctor, was a homeopath, who practised homeopathic medicine. He was not a surgeon, lawyer or teacher.
The snake coiled itself round his left arm, above the elbow. The doctor stayed frozen with fear.

quiz.q: What did the doctor think the sound was?
quiz.why: The doctor first thought the sound was a rat moving about in the room. In fact, it was a snake.

quiz.q: Whom did he dream of marrying?
quiz.why: He dreamed of marrying a rich, plump lady doctor, for comfort and wealth. This shows his vanity and daydreams.

options: The snake turned to the mirror and he slipped away
He jumped out of a window
quiz.why: The snake turned to look at the mirror, loosened its grip and moved away, so he slipped away. He did not kill it or jump out.

scenes.text: Uncle tells how he once posed for a selfie and fell into a pond.
Everyone laughs — and he laughs loudest. Basheer's doctor does the same.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Vanity**: the doctor is proud of his looks — and so, comically, is the snake.
- **Fear and presence of mind**: staying still saved his life.
- **Humility**: facing death makes him give up silly dreams.
- **Humour**: he laughs at himself.

steps.title: Sources of humour and irony
steps.body:
- The narrator calls himself handsome and plans a moustache like a model — self-mocking.
- He 'prays' to God and calls himself a 'stone image' — exaggeration.
- The snake admiring itself in the mirror mirrors the doctor's own vanity — **irony**.
- He suggests the snake may have been a lady snake, vain about its looks.
- His grand plan to marry a rich doctor collapses instantly.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **homeopath**: one who practises homeopathy
- **vain**: too proud of one's appearance
- **rafter**: sloping beam supporting a roof
- **petrified**: frozen with fear
- **plump**: pleasantly fat
- **fragrance**: pleasant smell

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Irony ≠ sarcasm: here irony is the **unexpected parallel** between the doctor and the snake.
- 'Vain' (proud of looks) vs 'vein' (blood vessel).

activity.prompt: Match the words

quiz.q: The main source of irony is:
options: The snake, like the doctor, seems to admire itself in the mirror
quiz.why: The irony is that the snake, like the doctor, seems to admire itself in the mirror. The doctor's vanity is mirrored in the snake.
'Petrified' means frozen with fear. The doctor was too scared to move.
The theme is vanity and humility, as the doctor's vanity is replaced by humility after the experience. It is not about war or patriotism.
The narrator's tone is humorous and self-mocking, as he laughs at his own foolish vanity. It is not angry or tragic.
'Vain' sounds like 'vein' and 'vane' but is spelled differently from both. These words are homophones.

scenes.text: Riya's friend asks, 'Why did the snake leave him?'
Riya explains step by step — exactly like an exam answer.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. Describe the doctor's state of mind when the snake coiled round his arm. (6 marks)**
The doctor was terrified. He realised any movement could provoke a bite, so he sat absolutely still, like a stone statue, holding his breath. His mind raced; he thought of death and prayed to God, the 'Merciful'. He lost all his pride, forgetting his dreams of a moustache and a rich wife. Yet he kept enough presence of mind not to panic. When the snake turned to the mirror, he quietly escaped. The experience humbled him and made him value life over vanity.

steps.title: Solved short answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the doctor give up his plan of marrying the lady doctor? (2 marks)** The brush with death made him realise how silly and vain his dreams were.

**Q2. What did the doctor find when he returned with neighbours? (2 marks)** The snake was no longer there; it had gone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Describing only events, not feelings, when asked about 'state of mind'.
- Forgetting the humour — mention the narrator's self-mocking tone when relevant.

steps.title: Presence of mind
steps.body: Real-life tip: if you meet a snake, stay still and move away slowly; call for help. Most snakes bite only when threatened.

activity.prompt: Complete the sentences
activity.text: The doctor sat as still as a stone ___. The snake turned to look into the ___. Later he gave up his dream of marrying a rich ___ doctor.

quiz.q: A 'state of mind' answer focuses on:
quiz.why: A 'state of mind' answer focuses on feelings and thoughts, such as fear or vanity. It is not about weather or dates.

options: Any movement could provoke a bite
quiz.why: He stayed still because any movement could provoke the snake to bite. Staying still was his best chance of survival.
His vanity disappeared after the frightening experience, and he became humble. It did not grow.

quiz.q: When neighbours came, the snake was:
quiz.why: When the neighbours came, the snake was gone, so it had already escaped. They found nothing.

quiz.q: Safe action if you see a snake:
options: Stay calm, move away slowly and get help
quiz.why: If you see a snake, stay calm, move away slowly and get help. Throwing stones, chasing or picking it up is dangerous.

story.title: Retell it as a news report

scenes.text: The class turns the story into a funny local news report: 'Snake Prefers Mirror to Doctor'.
They practise headlines, the 5 Ws and a quote from the 'victim'.

steps.title: Solved extract (paraphrased)
steps.body:
**Passage (paraphrased):** I was looking at myself in the mirror and thought I was rather handsome. I decided to shave daily and grow a thin moustache.
(a) Who is speaking? → The doctor (narrator).
(b) What does this show about him? → He is vain about his looks.
(c) What two decisions did he make? → To shave daily and grow a moustache.
(d) Find a word meaning 'good-looking'. → Handsome.

steps.title: Writing link: story writing
steps.body: Write a short story (150 words) beginning: 'The lights went out, and then I heard a strange sound…' Include a setting, a problem, a climax, and a resolution; use dialogue sparingly; give a title.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stories without a clear climax and resolution.
- Switching tenses — keep to past tense.

steps.title: About the author
steps.body: **Vaikom Muhammad Basheer** (1908–1994) was a celebrated Malayalam writer known for humour and simple style; this story is translated from Malayalam.

a.text: You are camping and see a snake near your tent.

choices.label: Throw stones at it
choices.feedback: Provoking a snake increases the risk of a bite.

choices.label: Stay still, then slowly move away and tell an adult

b.text: The snake rears up. You remember the doctor in the story stayed still.

c.text: The snake slides away into the bushes. A forest guard later relocates it safely.

quiz.q: In the extract, the doctor appears:
quiz.why: In the extract, the doctor appears vain, as he admires his own looks and imagines wealth and marriage. He is not humble at that stage.
Vaikom Muhammad Basheer wrote in Malayalam. The story was later translated into English.
A good story needs a setting, a problem, a climax and a resolution. Only dialogue or a title is not enough.
'Handsome' means good-looking. It is not a word for clever, strong or rich.
Stories are usually written in the past tense, since they tell of events that have happened. They are not mostly in imperative or questions.

questions.q: Author of 'The Snake and the Mirror':
questions.why: Vaikom Muhammad Basheer wrote 'The Snake and the Mirror'. Bond, Mansfield and Asimov wrote other works.

questions.q: The narrator was a:
questions.why: The narrator was a homeopath. He was not a snake charmer, policeman or teacher.

questions.q: The snake looked into the:
questions.why: The snake looked into the mirror, which seemed to admire itself. That gave the doctor a chance to escape.

questions.q: The room had:
questions.why: The room had no electricity, and only a kerosene lamp lit it. That is why the mirror's reflection mattered.

questions.q: The doctor decided to grow a:
questions.why: The doctor decided to grow a thin moustache, thinking it would make him look better. It was part of his vanity.

questions.q: He compared himself to a:
questions.why: The doctor compared himself to a stone image, as he sat frozen without moving. He was too afraid to stir.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The doctor survived. Reason (R): He stayed still and the snake was distracted by the mirror.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The doctor survived because he stayed still and the snake was distracted by the mirror.

questions.q: The story was originally written in:
questions.why: The story was originally written in Malayalam by Basheer. It was later translated into English.

questions.q: What is ironic about the snake?
options: It too seemed vain, admiring its reflection
questions.why: The snake too seemed vain, as it appeared to admire its reflection in the mirror. This mirrors the doctor's own vanity.

questions.q: Which word best describes the doctor before the incident?
questions.why: Before the incident the doctor was vain, proud of his looks. After it he became humble.

questions.q: Which change happened in the doctor?
questions.why: The doctor changed from vain to humble, as the frightening experience cured his vanity. He did not become richer or cowardly.

questions.q: Case: A friend boasts about his looks and then trips on stage. Which story moment is similar?
options: Doctor's daydream interrupted by a snake
questions.why: A friend boasting then tripping is like the doctor's daydream being cut short by a snake. Vanity is interrupted by an unexpected event.

questions.q: What does the narrator's tone show about him?
questions.why: The narrator laughs at his own foolishness, which shows he can laugh at himself. He is not bitter or boastful.

questions.q: Why did the doctor pray to God?
options: He feared death and felt helpless
questions.why: The doctor prayed to God because he feared death and felt helpless with the snake on his arm. It was not out of habit.

questions.q: The best lesson from the story is:
options: Vanity is foolish; presence of mind matters in danger
questions.why: The story shows that vanity is foolish, as the doctor's pride in his looks is exposed by the danger. It also shows that presence of mind, staying calm and still, helps in danger.

courses.title: Ch 6 · My Childhood
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's memories of growing up in Rameswaram — his family, his friends across religions, two teachers who showed prejudice and courage, and his first earnings.
outcomes: Learners can describe Kalam's family and early influences
Learners can explain the incidents of prejudice and how they were resolved
Learners can discuss secularism and social harmony
Learners can answer board questions with textual detail

scenes.text: In a big old house of limestone and brick in Rameswaram, a boy grows up in a loving, simple family.
His three best friends come from priestly Hindu families. Nobody at home thinks it unusual.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam** was born in **Rameswaram** (in the then Madras State, now Tamil Nadu) into a middle-class **Tamil Muslim** family. His father **Jainulabdeen** had little formal education or wealth but great **wisdom** and generosity; his mother **Ashiamma** was an ideal helpmate who fed many outsiders every day. They lived in an **ancestral house** built in the middle of the 19th century, of limestone and brick. The family lived simply, but provided all necessities.

Kalam's three close childhood friends were **Ramanadha Sastry**, **Aravindan** and **Sivaprakasan**, all from orthodox Hindu Brahmin families. As children they never felt any difference because of religion. Ramanadha Sastry was the son of **Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry**, the high priest of the **Rameswaram temple**. Kalam's family arranged boats with a special platform for carrying idols during the annual **Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam** ceremony. His mother and grandmother told bedtime stories from the **Ramayana** and the life of the Prophet.

steps.title: People in Kalam's childhood
steps.body:
- **Jainulabdeen** – father; wise, honest, self-disciplined.
- **Ashiamma** – mother; generous.
- **Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan, Sivaprakasan** – friends.
- **Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry** – high priest, father of Ramanadha.
- **Samsuddin** – cousin, newspaper distributor.
- **Sivasubramania Iyer** – science teacher.
- **Ahmed Jallaluddin** – later his brother-in-law (Kalam does not dwell on him here).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Describe Kalam's parents. (3 marks)** His father Jainulabdeen had little education or wealth but was wise, generous and disciplined; his mother Ashiamma was an ideal helpmate who fed many outsiders daily. Both gave Kalam a secure, value-rich childhood.

**Q2. What shows religious harmony in Kalam's childhood? (2 marks)** His best friends were Hindu Brahmins; his family helped in the Sita Rama Kalyanam festival; he heard stories from the Ramayana and from the life of the Prophet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Kalam's father's name is **Jainulabdeen**; mother **Ashiamma**.
- Rameswaram was in the **Madras State** then (now Tamil Nadu).
- His three friends were Hindus, not Muslims.

activity.prompt: Match the person to the description

quiz.why: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam was born in Rameswaram, an island town in Tamil Nadu. Ramanathapuram is the district headquarters where he later studied.
Kalam's mother was Ashiamma. She was a kind, generous woman who fed many people every day.
Kalam's three close friends came from orthodox Hindu Brahmin families, although he was Muslim. Their friendship shows communal harmony.

quiz.q: His family helped in which ceremony?
quiz.why: Kalam's family helped in the Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam ceremony by arranging boats to carry the idols to the marriage site. It shows a shared community life.

quiz.q: Kalam's ancestral house was made of:
quiz.why: Kalam's ancestral house was built of limestone and brick. It was a fairly large house on Mosque Street in Rameswaram.

lessons.title: First earnings and the Second World War

scenes.text: 1939: suddenly tamarind seeds are in demand. Young Kalam collects them and sells them to a shop for an anna a day.
Then his cousin gives him a job catching newspaper bundles thrown from a moving train.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
When the **Second World War** broke out in **1939**, Kalam was about eight. For some reason, there was a sudden demand for **tamarind seeds**. He collected the seeds and sold them to a provision shop on Mosque Street — earning **one anna** a day.

The train halt at Rameswaram station was suspended because of the war, so newspapers had to be bundled and **thrown out from the moving train** on the Rameswaram–Dhanuskodi route. His cousin **Samsuddin**, who distributed newspapers, needed help to catch the bundles, and Kalam filled the slot. He says he earned his **first wages** this way, and remembers the pride half a century later.

Kalam notes that every child is born, with some inherited characteristics, into a specific socio-economic and emotional environment, and is shaped by authority figures. From his father he learned **honesty and self-discipline**; from his mother **faith in goodness and deep kindness** — as did his three brothers and sister.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Kalam earn his first wages? (2 marks)** By helping his cousin Samsuddin catch newspaper bundles thrown from the moving train during WWII.
